question: For a simple undirected graph with N vertices given by its adjacency matrix A: (1) what does the entry (A^k)_{ij} represent, (2) how can one determine from A whether the graph is connected, and (3) what is the definition of a path between vertices n_i and n_j?

sources.notes: Course textbook. Title page says 214 pages (brief says 216, which is the PDF page count). Printed page = PDF page minus 1; all locators here are printed pages. I viewed page images of printed pp. 11, 21, 22, 23, 48, 49 and read the text layer of pp. 16 and 22 to 23. The text layer drops symbols, so quotes with formulas were copied from the page image and may differ from the text layer in spacing. Book calls a walk 'shrjanc'um', a trail 'chanaparh' (Definition 1.2.12) and a path 'parz chanaparh' (Definition 1.2.13). Per-page text-layer search for the word matrix finds adjacency matrix only on printed pp. 7, 11, 12, 34, 61 (other hits are incidence, total unimodularity and general uses). Not read: the rest of the book. Original textbook, not a review.

sources.venue: arXiv:2308.04512v3 [math.HO], Spring 2025 edition dated June 7, 2025 (text for Math 530, Drexel University)
sources.notes: Downloaded the full PDF (454 pages) from arxiv.org/pdf/2308.04512 and read Section 2.9 (walks, paths, connectivity for simple graphs), Theorem 4.5.10 with its proof, and the BFS passage. Page numbers are the printed page numbers in the running header of the June 7, 2025 version; they may differ in other versions. Theorem 4.5.10 is stated for multidigraphs, so its use for simple undirected graphs needs the one-step argument that each edge gives two arcs (see claim C5). Lecture-notes text, not peer reviewed; version 3 of a long-lived arXiv text. Original exposition, not a review.

claims.text: Test: a simple graph on N >= 2 vertices is connected if and only if every off-diagonal entry of A + A^2 + ... + A^(N-1) is positive; equivalently (I + A)^(N-1) has no zero entry. Proof: (A^k)_{ij} counts walks (C5); a walk gives a path of no greater length (C17) and a path has length at most N - 1 (C18); expanding (I + A)^(N-1) by the binomial theorem gives a sum of I and the powers A^k with positive coefficients. Not proved in any source read in the form (I + A)^(N-1).

claims.text: Walk-counting theorem: for a simple undirected graph and every integer k >= 0, (A^k)_{ij} equals the number of walks of length k from n_i to n_j (A^0 = I, the identity matrix). Proof by induction on k: the base case k = 0, and the step splits a walk of length k+1 at its last vertex before the end. Because the graph is simple, a walk is determined by its vertex sequence. The textbook has no such theorem (see C9); the proof is the paper's own, and Grinberg Theorem 4.5.10 states the multidigraph version.

claims.text: In a simple graph a walk (textbook Definition 1.2.10) is determined by its sequence of vertices, since each edge e_i = u_{i-1}u_i is fixed by its two ends; hence a walk of length k is a vertex sequence u_0, ..., u_k in which consecutive vertices are adjacent, and the length counts edges with repetition. claims.text: In a simple graph a walk is determined by its vertex sequence u_0, u_1, ..., u_k, because the edge u_{i-1}u_i is the only edge between those two vertices. So a walk of length k from n_i to n_j is the same data as a sequence of k+1 vertices with consecutive vertices adjacent. The textbook abbreviates a walk by its vertex sequence in the same way; Grinberg defines a walk for simple graphs as the vertex sequence.
